echoes.note: Paul reasons in the synagogue 'every Sabbath' (v.4); the rhythm of weekly Sabbath gathering presupposes the Decalogue's Sabbath command. Faint and institutional rather than verbal, but the Sabbath frame is the OT scaffolding for the scene.

Paul stays with Aquila and Priscilla and works as a tentmaker (vv.2-3), earning bread by the labor of his own hands. A faint resonance with the Edenic decree of toil/sweat; the motif of apostolic self-support by manual labor draws on the dignity-and-burden-of-work theme rooted here.

Paul 'shook out his clothing' (garment) as a prophetic sign-act against those who oppose him — directly mirroring Nehemiah shaking out the fold of his robe as a curse-gesture: 'So may God shake out everyone... who does not perform this promise.' A symbolic disavowal handing the consequences back on the offenders.

'Your blood be on your own heads! I am clean' transposes the watchman oracle: the warned who ignore the trumpet bear their own blood, while the faithful watchman has delivered his soul. Paul casts himself as the discharged watchman, his hearers as the warned-but-unheeding.
The watchman who warns the wicked and is not heeded 'has delivered his soul' — exactly Paul's claim 'I am clean.' Recurrence with Ezekiel 33:4 strengthens the watchman frame.

The original commissioning of the watchman: if he warns and the wicked does not turn, 'you will have delivered your soul.' Paul's 'I am clean / your blood on your heads' draws on this earlier statement of the same principle.
'Your blood be on your own head' is David's verdict on the Amalekite — the same idiom of self-incurred bloodguilt that Paul pronounces over the resisting synagogue.
The recurring legal formula 'his blood shall be upon him' (cf. vv.11-13,16,27) is the juridical source of the 'blood on your own head' idiom of self-responsibility that Paul invokes.
Rahab's covenant: anyone who goes out of the house, 'his blood shall be on his own head,' while the household is held guiltless — the same shifting-of-bloodguilt formula behind Paul's declaration.
'His blood shall be upon himself' in the chapter on individual responsibility reinforces the bloodguilt idiom underlying Paul's words.

The night-vision reassurance 'Do not be afraid... for I am with you' is the classic divine-encouragement formula, of which Isaiah 41:10 ('Fear not, for I am with you... I will strengthen you') is the paradigm. Paul stands in the line of those summoned and steadied by God's presence.

Jeremiah's prophetic call: 'Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you.' Paul's commission to keep speaking despite opposition echoes the prophet's reassurance against hostile hearers.
'They will fight against you but will not prevail, for I am with you' closely matches 'no one will attack you to harm you, for I am with you' — the same promise of protected speech in a hostile city.
'I will be with you' grounds Moses' sending; the same assurance underwrites Paul's mission in Corinth. The call-narrative pattern (objection met by promise of presence) shapes the vision.

Closest single parallel: the LORD appears to Isaac by night and says, 'Do not be afraid, for I am with you... I will multiply your offspring.' Night theophany + 'fear not' + 'I am with you' + promise of a great people maps almost point-for-point onto vv.9-10, including 'I have many people in this city.'
'Do not be frightened... for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go' — the commissioning encouragement to a leader facing a daunting task, reused for Paul.
'Do not fear... for the LORD your God goes with you; he will not leave you' belongs to the same 'fear not / I am with you' tradition behind the vision.
'Fear not, for I am with you' paired with gathering a people resonates with both the reassurance and the promise of 'many people in this city.'

Paul is haled before the tribunal by accusers who 'rose up' with malicious charges — the lament motif of malicious witnesses rising against the righteous sufferer ('Malicious witnesses rise up; they ask me of things I do not know').
The concerted false accusation 'with one accord' before the judgment seat faintly recalls the law against joining a multitude to bring a malicious/false charge.

Paul 'shaved his head in Cenchreae, for he had a vow' — the Nazirite practice of shaving the head at the completion/discharge of a vow. Numbers 6:18 specifies shaving the consecrated head; the detail marks Paul's continued observance of Torah piety.

The Nazirite law that no razor touch the head during the vow's duration (the hair grown then shaved) underlies the haircut-as-vow-completion in v.18. Recurrence with Numbers 6:18 anchors the Nazirite frame.
Paul's resolve to 'keep this coming feast in Jerusalem' (v.21) reflects the pilgrimage-feast obligation to appear before the LORD at the appointed feasts in Jerusalem.
The thrice-yearly command to appear before the Lord undergirds Paul's intention to keep the feast in Jerusalem; faint and institutional.

Apollos, 'mighty in the Scriptures,' speaks boldly in the synagogue and publicly refutes opponents from Scripture — resonating with the psalmist's resolve to 'speak of your testimonies before kings and not be put to shame.' Faint thematic, no verbal borrowing.
